sections.content: For the purpose of layoff of employees, seniority shall be defined as the length of continuous service with the County of Niagara. However, service as a regular permanent part-time employee shall be pro-rated based on the number of hours worked by the regular permanent part-time employee as compared to the hours of work as a full-time employee. The formula used to determine the number of years of full-time service of a regular permanent part-time employee shall be as follows: Annual number of hours worked by a regular permanent part-time employee divided by the annual number of hours worked by a full-time employee. Figure gained from this computation shall then be multiplied by the years of service an employee has as a regular permanent part-time employee. The resulting number of years of service shall be used to determine the number of years of service a part-time employee has for layoff, and/or added to the years of service of an employee who has since become a full-time employee.

sections.content: GENERAL PROVISIONS

Testing will be performed by an outside agency, in order that impartiality and confidentiality are ensured. Both the drug and alcohol tests will be conducted by certified professionals. In both instances, confirmation tests will be conducted should the initial test prove positive. In the case of alcohol testing, all testing shall be done by breathalyzer, and/or blood test. In the case of the drug test, specimen collection may be observed if the testing agency deems it necessary, and all specimens will be separated into two (2) samples. If the initial sample is positive, then the employee has the right to request that the split sample be tested at a laboratory of his/her choosing (within 72 hours of being notified by the Medical Review Officer), at the employee's expense. However, if the results of the second test show the initial test results to be a false positive, the County will assume the cost of the second test and the employee will be reimbursed for any work time lost based on action taken on the first sample results. The County shall pay all costs associated with the administration of the alcohol tests.

category_summaries.summary: Recognition provisions establish the County of Niagara as the exclusive negotiating agent for all full-time and regular part-time white-collar employees in Niagara County, New York, with “white-collar employees” defined as those holding positions listed in the Appendix. Regular permanent part-time employees are defined as employees working 17.5 hours or more per week, and the County extends unchallenged representation status to the Civil Service Employees Association (CSEA) for the maximum period permitted by law. Where CSEA is recognized or certified as the exclusive representative for the bargaining unit, the County will deduct fees from non-member employees’ wages/salaries (bi-weekly deductions remitted monthly to CSEA at 143 Washington Avenue, Albany, NY 12210) and the fiscal/disbursing officer will transmit the amounts determined by the employees’ employment status (part-time or full-time) and as established by CSEA. Such remitted fees must be accompanied by a list of non-member employees’ names and addresses, sent to the Article address specified in Section “1,” and union representatives must be notified of the distribution of this information.

The contract’s effectiveness and operation are subject to several duration-related controls: provisions found contrary to law are not deemed valid, and the parties must meet immediately to negotiate lawful replacements. The agreement is effective only upon approval by the appropriate legislative body and takes effect on January 1, 2000. Leave of absence without pay cannot extend beyond four (4) years from the date the employee left the competitive class position, and any extension beyond six (6) months may be requested if necessary and will not be unreasonably denied. Administrative timing also applies, including the requirement that the County provide the Committee with ninety (90) days’ notice if it wishes to change the Program’s Third Party Administrator (TPA). Current exceptions to the policy are grandfathered into existing terms. Contract duration is further protected by rules that amendments must be in writing, verbal or informal agreements cannot modify the contract (except a written amendment), and modifications in whole or part are prohibited; remaining articles are not affected.

Management retains all authority, rights, and responsibilities of the County, including determining the County’s mission, purpose, objectives, and policies; selecting facilities, methods, means, and the number of personnel for County programs; administering the merit system (including examinations, selection, recruitment, hiring, appraisal, training, retention, promotion, assignment, or transfer in accordance with law); directing, deploying, and utilizing the workforce; and disciplining or discharging employees in accordance with applicable law and the Agreement. The County has the exclusive right to schedule work and control/regulate the use of equipment and property, subject to operational requirements that allow work schedules to be altered by department needs. The County may create and/or abolish positions, determine departmental/operational needs, and determine the number of employees required for services, including any required negotiation of the impact with the Union. The County may also change timekeeping systems at its sole discretion, but will provide two (2) weeks’ notice of its intent to implement and/or change such timekeeping systems; any vacancy postings are for information only and do not obligate the County to fill vacancies.

Compensation includes weekly pay at 50% of gross pay up to $170/week, with overtime paid at time-and-one-half for required work, except that an employee working the actual holiday and the holiday-celebration day may receive time-and-one-half for only one of those days and will receive one compensatory day off or may elect pay in lieu. Additional shift and standby premiums include 2.5× the hourly rate for each hour in additional 8-hour shift(s); double time for ordered night standby, plus for weekend standby one full day either in cash or time off; and shift differentials of $0.30/hour (second shift) and $0.35/hour (third shift), plus an additional $0.30/hour for hours after 3:00 PM for scheduled shifts starting after 9:00 AM–5:00 PM, subject to application rules to absences (except vacations/extended absences) and sick-pay timing after eight consecutive absent days. Overtime/comp-time mechanics provide time-and-one-half for hours over 40/week, with employees paid at the regular hourly rate for hours 35–40/week, and (when electing comp time) a maximum accumulation of 240 hours (with bank freezing for balances as of Dec. 1, 1993 and payment for overtime if the bank is at/above 240). Salary administration provides bi-weekly Friday pay (preceding day if holiday), IRS-governed mileage reimbursement, and other pay adjustments for promotion/demotion/reinstatement and temporary higher-group assignments, including eligibility and hour thresholds for higher-rate step-for-step pay (and parity-only for hours beyond the 70/80-hour threshold within a fiscal year). Increment eligibility generally requires time in service (including minimum six months worked during any calendar year while on unpaid leave), with increments granted up to the maximum for the position and timing rules (e.g., pre–July 1 hires eligible for Jan. 1 following; others require a full calendar year). Longevity payments apply after consecutive paid employment: 10 years; 14 years (additional $275 for total $500/year); 20 years (additional $325 for total $825/year); and 25 years (additional $325 for total $1,150/year), pro-rated and paid in 26 equal payments. The agreement also provides annual general wage increases: 1998 ($0.64/hour), 1999 (4%), 2000 (added to salary/hourly rate), and 2001 (4%). Alcohol-test administration costs are paid by the County; employees are reimbursed for any work time lost, and all time spent (including travel) is paid at regular or overtime rate if applicable, with employees kept on payroll until the time a positive test occurs.

Scheduling provisions establish that a regular employee’s normal work week runs Monday through Friday, with hours/shift assignments and regular starting and quitting times set by the department head. The County will provide reasonable advance notice (except for emergencies) and will notify CSEA of required scheduling changes; it may not temporarily alter an employee’s normal shift to avoid overtime. Employees receive an uninterrupted lunch break, and if an emergency interrupts it, they may resume after the emergency to complete the full break; compensatory time off is provided equal to the remaining time in the lunch break. Full-time employees on an eight (8) hour day are entitled to two (2) paid fifteen (15) minute breaks during the second four (4) hours (with the second break including smoking time), while seven (7) hour day employees receive two (2) paid fifteen (15) minute breaks—one in the first three and one-half (3-1/2) hours and one in the second three and one-half (3-1/2) hours (smoking time included in the second). Permanent regular part-time employees working at least four (4) consecutive hours get one (1) fifteen (15) minute break during the shift. For call-in coverage, the effective period runs from the end of the employee’s regular shift on a work day until the start of the next regular shift, with the call-in terms renewing each time the employee is called; employees are generally guaranteed a minimum of two (2) hours per day and must punch in/out if required. The County will distribute overtime as equitably as possible (including considering all paid leave time/holidays as time worked for overtime calculations), employees may refuse overtime (with refused hours still charged as time worked for overtime equalization), second and third shifts will be paid at least one (1) day prior to first shift when possible, and any new scheduling/punching system must be uniformly applied to all bargaining unit members.

Leave provisions cover (1) Association business leave: officers/delegates may take up to 26 days off yearly to attend business meetings, with no County pay; they may, at their option, charge the leave to accrued vacation/personal/compensatory credits (but sick leave may not be used for meeting attendance). The Union President may use 1 paid day per week for union business (with the same benefit for a designee if the President is in paid leave). (2) Sick leave: may be used for the employee’s sickness, immediate family illness (including medical/dental visits), with a physician statement requested when family illness causes absence over 3 consecutive work days; personal illness absence must be reported by the first working day within 1/2 hour of start time, and Saturday absence is not charged unless Saturday is a working day. Sick leave accrues at 1 working day per month, is cumulative to 185 days, based on a January 1 year, and credits generally do not accrue while on leave of absence without pay, under disciplinary punishment causing loss of work time, or on disability; time on full-rate payroll counts as “served.” Sick leave may be used in one-hour increments (with beginning-of-shift use in half-day increments unless prior approval is granted for verifiable doctor/dental visits). Medical/dental sick-leave use is discretionary as to department head approval, limited to 8 visits per calendar year, with each visit limited to 2 hours, and absences over 2 hours are charged in 1/2-day units. (3) Disability/other leave and credit effects: sick/vacation credits do not accrue while receiving just disability benefits; instead, employees may earn 1/2 vacation day and 1/2 sick day if on active payroll for over half the workdays in a month, and service is treated as uninterrupted. Employees may receive payment for 25% of unused accumulated sick days upon retirement. Benefits are available for 26 weeks in any 52-week period, with a waiting period of 5 working days or 7 calendar days (whichever is less) after injury/illness before drawing benefits, during which employees may use accumulated sick time; sick time while receiving benefits must be in half-day increments. (4) Bereavement and other paid/unpaid leaves: bereavement leave is up to 3 consecutive regularly scheduled workdays with pay, with the County HR able to reschedule within documented reasonable individualized needs; eligibility requires attending the funeral/memorial service, and rules address counting the day of death report-in, Saturday scheduling, and adding 3 paid days if death occurs during vacation. Immediate-family death triggers additional paid bereavement coverage per the defined immediate family list. A separate full-pay leave of up to 6 months is provided in special circumstances, followed by potential unpaid extension up to an additional 12 months; on return, consumed credits are reaccredited proportionally, and accrued leave is paid. (5) Personal/vacation leave and accrual/pay limits: employees may earn/discuss personal leave day eligibility after 90 days; personal business requires a written request at least 3 days prior, is not allowed on the day before/after a holiday or in conjunction with vacation except at the department head’s discretion, may be disapproved, and remaining personal days are added to sick accumulation (unused personal days are not paid upon termination). Vacation leave includes holiday pay eligibility conditions (paid status the day before and day after, excluding floating holiday rules), conversion of unused vacation to sick leave when unused due to disability, and carryover pursuant to the referenced agreement article. Vacation accrual is based on the fiscal year as the calendar year, with “month worked” meaning active payroll for at least half the workdays; vacations are earned but not cumulative, must generally be taken in the calendar year due, and department approval governs timing and transfers. Vacation is earned for new employees at 1 day per month up to 10 days, and thereafter scheduled by service length (e.g., 15 days after 5 years, 17 after 8 years). Upon separation/retirement/resignation/layoff, unused vacation is paid out; no vacation accumulates while absent; discharged employees under Section 75 receive no vacation credit for the discharge year (but may receive previously earned, unused credit). Unpaid leave may be granted for family/medical/military purposes (typically up to 1 year at appointing authority discretion, renewable with approvals), adopted-child care up to 6 months (no section total exceeding 12 months), and child rearing up to 10 months unpaid upon notification; jury duty is provided as required by NY law with compensation of the difference between jury pay and normal daily pay; continuous leave without pay generally may not exceed 12 months without Personnel Officer approval.

Healthcare benefits are provided to regular permanent part-time employees and other eligible bargaining-unit members, including employer-paid medical coverage under the Niagara County Health Care Plan, with hospitalization and medical-surgical coverage. For employees hired on/after September 1, 1982, the employee must pay 50% of the cost of the Niagara County Health Plan; additionally, employees hired after January 1, 1990 must pay 100% of health care premiums for the first six (6) months of county employment, after which the employee generally pays 50% and the employer pays 100% of the health insurance program. The County guarantees the Niagara County Health Plan benefit levels as of January 1, 1998, sets plan costs based on the county’s annually established independent audit rates, and may select the disability insurance provider. The County agrees to provide a minimum statutory disability insurance plan registered with New York State to employees with four consecutive weeks of continuous service, with negotiation of cost-containment if yearly premium increases exceed 25% (e.g., longer waiting periods or greater use of leave accruals before eligibility). Employees may opt in/out of the Niagara County Health Plan with restrictions: opting out prevents re-enrollment in GHI, current non-enrolled employees cannot select GHI in future open enrollment, and new employees cannot choose GHI as an alternative. Employees who opt out and later lose alternate coverage may be reinstated as soon as possible. The County pays for only one family plan (or two single plans if permitted) when both spouses are County employees. A health insurance premium offset/waiver payment may be available in two equal installments (July 1 and December), but requires proof of other health insurance at application, and eligibility is tied to the County contribution rate and maximum waiver amount. Retiree coverage is available for employees retiring on/after January 1, 1990 under the current plan (prior retirees maintain coverage), subject to maintaining Medicare Part A and B where eligible; retirees (not spouses) receive biannual reimbursement of Medicare Part B premiums. Finally, the County deposits $100 per employee into a flexible spending account for Optical and/or Dental care.

Under the Ancillary-related provisions, employees are required to contribute $0.60 per week toward disability insurance costs. Time off payroll is not credited toward retirement, which is defined as retirement under the New York State Retirement System. The County must provide the 1/60th plan retroactive to 1938, and commencing April 1, 1971, adopt Plan 75-G with Riders 41-J and 60-B. The County will also adopt Plan 75-I for all bargaining unit members in Tiers 1 and 2 of the New York State Retirement System. Bargaining unit members may participate in an existing deferred compensation plan, administered by Equi-Comp, and the County will adjust payroll as needed to permit participation; the plan must be made available to all bargaining unit employees. Additionally, the County will deposit into a flexible spending account either $150 or $200 per employee (as stated in separate provisions).

Seniority is generally based on an employee’s length of continuous service with the County of Niagara, including all approved leaves of absence (and, for benefits purposes, time worked as a regular permanent part-time employee). Unpaid and disability leaves do not interrupt continuous service, but they reduce earned seniority. Continuous service is limited to periods on the County’s active payroll, except for other periods that Civil Service Law requires to be treated as continuous service. Regular permanent part-time years of service for layoff are pro-rated using the formula: (annual hours worked by the part-time employee ÷ annual hours worked by a full-time employee) multiplied by the employee’s years as a regular permanent part-time employee. Layoffs are conducted by seniority within the job classification (with temporary, provisional, and probationary employees in the department/job classification laid off first), where the least senior employee in the classification is laid off first, and the laid-off employee may use seniority to displace employees in lower rated job titles; recall occurs in inverse order of layoff, with senior employees recalled if qualified. Laid-off employees are placed on a recall list for up to four (4) years and have recall rights for four (4) years from the date of last layoff, and employees on layoff in the class title are recalled by reverse seniority. The County must meet with CSEA to review anticipated layoffs at least 30 calendar days before the action, and employees to be laid off must receive 14 calendar days’ notice. Employees lose all service and seniority rights if they leave County service without an approved leave of absence (unless reinstated within applicable Civil Service Law periods), and employees rehired after January 1, 1970 do not receive credit for prior County service. Separately, certain transfer/authorization rules apply (e.g., job descriptions upon request, transfer requests within 10 days of vacancy announcement, transfers not for disciplinary reasons, credits transfer with the employee, intra-departmental transfers by a department head, and for involuntary permanent transfers, 5 working days’ notice).

Training obligations include assessing an employee’s usefulness to the department. Required training must be provided through a course offered by a recognized college, university, or school. The Director of Human Resources (or their designee) is responsible for arranging training for all Department Heads, and Department Heads must participate in a certified training program that has been approved by the EAP Administrator.

The agreement provides a detailed grievance and dispute-resolution process. Newly hired/reinstated/transferred/terminated employees must be reported to CSEA within thirty (30) days after each pay period. Disputes over representation/coverage for any newly created titles (and any omitted existing titles) are resolved through the Public Employment Relations Board. Grievances must be raised first within twenty (20) working days of the occurrence, initially through a Union steward or elected Union officer (and only one steward per department may conduct investigations), with written notice stating the nature of the grievance and the specific contract provisions alleged violated. Stewards may investigate during working hours with notice and permission from their immediate superior, without loss of pay/time, for up to one (1) hour per day unless additional time is reasonably needed; department heads must not arbitrarily withhold permission and stewards must not abuse the right. Communications must be sent to the Chairperson of the Association Grievance Committee (and the grievant). Failure by the department head to issue a decision within the designated time limits allows the grievant to proceed to the next stage; failure to comply or certain improper actions can constitute withdrawal and bar further action. Time spent presenting grievances is not charged against leave. The procedure is intended to resolve issues at the lowest administrative level in good faith, with fair opportunity and no interference with county operations; Civil Service Law charges by department heads are not grounds for grievances. Where the employee/Union seeks review of disputed claims or duplicate denials, notice must be given within thirty (30) working days; Risk Management reviews within twenty (20) working days, with an appeal form submitted within twenty (20) working days, followed by a final written decision by a neutral panel within ten (10) working days, with equal sharing of costs. For labor management meetings, a request may be made and the meeting scheduled within ten (10) days of request (via the Human Resources Director). Disciplinary matters tied to alcohol/drug policy violations follow the agreement’s discharge/discipline provisions and use a progressive, case-by-case review, including periodic reports where a rehabilitation program is required; one specified discipline includes thirty (30) days suspension and mandatory EAP. For reasonable suspicion testing, the Union President must receive a complete listing of all tested bargaining-unit members, and any challenge to negative reasonable suspicion testing must proceed through Stage 3 of the grievance/arbitration mechanism, where the arbitrator may award up to one day’s pay to the employee.

The County will maintain workplace safety and health during working hours and requires department heads and employees to cooperate in implementing reasonable safety provisions, including joint obligations to prevent unsafe practices and accidents. Department heads must report and review violations of safety-related obligations, and incidents that could lead to harm (including unsafe conditions) should be witnessed and documented in writing immediately. The County must provide workers’ compensation insurance and continue reasonable and necessary safety/health measures; employees are also required to cooperate and violations are reported to the department head. In parallel, the agreement prohibits using, distributing, dispensing, possessing, or manufacturing illegal drugs on job sites or county property, prohibits discrimination, and bars harassment related to the drug/alcohol policy. Separately, employees who reasonably believe an action/incident may lead to a claim against them or the County must report it in writing to their immediate supervisor within seventy-two (72) hours. Drug and alcohol testing is limited to reasonable-suspicion testing: testing may be ordered only by a trained department head who has reasonable suspicion of prohibited drug/alcohol use. The prohibited substances are Marijuana, Cocaine, Amphetamines, Opiates (including heroin), and Phencyclidine (PCP). Alcohol testing uses breathalyzer and/or blood tests, and the Medical Review Officer must notify employees so they can request a split-sample test at a laboratory of their choosing within seventy-two (72) hours (at the employee’s expense). Test results and records are strictly confidential and cannot be released except to a substance abuse professional with the employee’s written consent; treatment records for alcoholism/drug problems remain separate from other personnel files. Refusal to submit to a test may result in discipline, and employees suspected of being unfit for duty must not remain at the workplace (including that impaired employees should not be allowed to drive home). The County and department heads will be trained to recognize reasonable-suspicion behaviors, which include specified signs of impairment, and the Director of Human Resources will provide employees with copies of the policy and educational materials and information on an Employee Assistance Program (EAP); employees who test positive may volunteer for evaluation through the EAP.

The Union affirms it will not strike against any government and will not engage in concerted stoppages of work or slowdowns; the County may not lock out employees or prevent employees from entering designated work sites and performing job duties. The Agreement supersedes conflicting employer rules. Within 30 days after ratification, the County must furnish CSEA a complete list of unit employees’ names, home addresses, Social Security numbers, work locations, and position titles. The Association must hold the employer harmless from claims/liability, with such losses treated as the employer’s responsibility, and the County agrees to indemnify/bargaining-unit members against financial loss arising out of defense; employees involved in potentially litigious incidents must cooperate with the County Attorney, and the County is not obligated under certain coverage unless an employee acts within 10 days. The Association may inspect Civil Service eligibility lists upon request; contacting new employees requires supervisor permission, not unreasonably withheld. CSEA may designate insurance representatives who coordinate with department heads on mutually agreed times to explain benefits. A Vance Committee (up to three members) is formed with a majority from participating unions, and a Joint Committee participates in developing bid/quote standards for a new Third Party Administrator, evaluates bids/quotes, and recommends and ranks administrators. Miscellany also includes: no lock/claim adjustment by the County for all or part of an award; discharged employees receive no termination benefits except as provided elsewhere; CSEA may use designated exclusive bulletin board space and cannot be challenged by other organizations’ postings (with removal of any County-objected material); personnel files are limited to attendance and work performance and must not include derogatory information unless provided in writing to the employee, while such information must be provided to employees on a three-day request (one per month). Additional items include: limited driving home in a County vehicle by a department head; split samples may be tested at a laboratory chosen by the employee; an EAP screens employees and determines whether treatment is necessary; the testing policy will not take effect until an EAP is in place, and nothing construes denial of CBA rights or permits the County to unilaterally change policy terms/procedures.
